overview:
At eleven o'clock on the night of 31 January 2020, the United Kingdom ceased to be a member state of the European Union, ending forty-seven years inside the bloc and its predecessor institutions. The vote that set this in motion had been held in June 2016, but the three and a half years between the referendum and the exit consumed two prime ministers, three extensions of the Article 50 deadline, and a Parliament that repeatedly refused to ratify the terms on offer. The deadlock broke with the general election of December 2019, which returned Boris Johnson with a majority of eighty seats and a mandate to pass the withdrawal agreement he had renegotiated. The European Union (Withdrawal Agreement) Act cleared Parliament in January 2020, and departure followed within weeks.

Leaving was not, however, a single moment. The withdrawal agreement settled the terms of divorce — the rights of EU citizens in Britain and Britons on the continent, a financial settlement, and a protocol keeping Northern Ireland aligned with EU goods rules so that no hard border would return on the island of Ireland — and then suspended nearly all practical change for an eleven-month transition. Through 2020 the UK remained in the single market and the customs union, still bound by EU law and the European Court of Justice, but with no commissioner, no MEPs, and no seat at the Council table. Negotiations on the future relationship ran the length of that year against a pandemic, and the government legislated to forbid itself from seeking an extension past the July deadline. The EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement was agreed on 24 December 2020 and applied provisionally from the first minute of 2021; the real rupture — customs declarations, regulatory checks, the end of free movement — arrived that night, not in January.

The dataset holds one event beneath this story, and it is a small and characteristic one: the Wooferendum, a campaign founded by Daniel Elkan that brought dog owners and their animals to central London to demand a second referendum, marching in October 2018 and staging a "dog's dinner" protest outside Parliament in March 2019. It was a joke with a serious core. Pet passports had abolished six-month quarantine in 2000; a large share of British veterinary staff were EU nationals; pet food and medicines moved on continental supply chains. The Wooferendum belongs to the enormous, inventive, and ultimately unsuccessful Remain protest culture of 2018 and 2019 — a reminder that Brexit was argued out not only in the Commons and in Brussels but in the specific, domestic anxieties of people who could not see how the new arrangements would touch their own lives.
significance: This was the first time a member state had left the European Union, and it settled a question the treaties had left largely theoretical: the bloc could be exited, but only slowly, expensively, and at the cost of trade friction that no free trade agreement fully removes. For the United Kingdom it reopened constitutional questions that had seemed closed — the status of Northern Ireland, whose protocol created a regulatory border in the Irish Sea and became a running source of instability, and the place of Scotland, which had voted heavily to remain. For the EU it hardened the remaining twenty-seven around a common negotiating position and made departure a far less attractive prospect for other eurosceptic movements. The Office for Budget Responsibility's working assumption, that the new relationship would leave UK imports and exports around fifteen per cent lower and long-run productivity about four per cent lower than continued membership, remains contested, but the direction of the estimate has framed British economic argument ever since.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, the Institute for Government's transition-period explainer, and search results summarizing the OBR's forecasting assumptions; attempts to retrieve the House of Commons Library Brexit timeline and the European Council's own chronology were blocked, so precise procedural dates here are secondary rather than primary. The dataset holds only one event under this story — the Wooferendum, a minor protest — so the map's coverage is far thinner than the record, which is exceptionally well documented in Hansard, EU institutional archives, and contemporary journalism. Economic estimates of Brexit's effects are genuinely disputed among economists rather than settled, and the counterfactual is unobservable; the figures cited are one respected body's assumptions, not measurements.
